cues.text: A Voice from Legend and Devotion
St. Cecilia has been venerated in Rome since at least the fifth century, when Pope Gelasius entered her name into the calendar of the Roman Church.
Her story, as it has come down to us through the Acts of St. Cecilia , belongs to that precious body of early Christian memory.
In it, historical fact and devotional legend are woven closely together.
We do well to receive her story as the early Church received it, not as a court record to be cross-examined.
Instead, it is a treasured memory of holiness, shaped by generations of faithful love, through which a real martyr of ancient Rome continues to speak to us.
A Consecrated Heart

According to this tradition, Cecilia was a young noblewoman of Rome who had privately consecrated her virginity to God, only to find herself given in marriage, by her family's arrangement, to a pagan youth named Valerian .
On their wedding night, we are told, amid the music of the celebration, her heart sang to the Lord alone.
She confided to her new husband that an angel of God watched over her, guarding a purity that could not be violated.
Moved by her witness, Valerian sought out the aged Pope Urban, hidden among the poor along the Appian Way during a time of persecution.
There, he received baptism, returning to find Cecilia's promise confirmed and to embrace, alongside her, a marriage of shared consecration rather than ordinary union.
A Family Won for Christ
Valerian in turn won over his own brother Tiburtius to the faith.
The two brothers devoted themselves to burying Christians martyred in the day’s persecutions, a perilous charity.
They were soon arrested and put to death.
Cecilia, refusing to abandon the mission her husband and brother-in-law had begun, continued to preach and to convert as her own arrest drew near.
Tradition tells us she won hundreds more to the faith in the short time that remained to her—a chain of witness passed from heart to heart, exactly as the Gospel itself has always spread.
Three Days of Dying, and of Giving
Condemned to death by suffocation in the baths of her own house, Cecilia is said to have survived unharmed.
The executioner sent to behead her struck three blows without severing her head.
Roman law forbidding a fourth stroke, he left her to die slowly of her wounds.
For three days, we are told, she lingered and used this final gift of time as she had used every other gift of her life.
She distributed her remaining possessions to the poor and commended her house to the Church, that it might become, as it still is today, a place of worship.
When her tomb was opened in 1599, her body was reported to be remarkably well preserved and lying on its side, hands folded in prayer, precisely as later artists have immortalized her ever since.
The Song That Has Never Ceased
Though the connection between Cecilia and music arose, historically, from a later and rather poetic reading of her wedding-night prayer, the Church has embraced this association for centuries.
It has done so with evident joy, and rightly so.
What could more fittingly crown the memory of a woman who gave her whole heart, unseen, to God alone?
She became patroness of the art by which the human heart most freely lifts its unseen depths toward heaven.
Since the founding of the Roman Academy of Music under her patronage in 1585, Cecilian societies of sacred music have flourished across the world.

Composers from Palestrina to Britten have set her memory to sound, so that the silent song she is said to have sung in her heart on her wedding night has become, in the centuries since, an unceasing chorus.
Legacy

Cecilia's name has been spoken at every Mass in the Roman Canon since ancient times, standing among the small company of women martyrs the Church holds in special honor alongside the Apostles themselves.
Her basilica in Trastevere, believed to stand upon the very site of her home, remains a place of pilgrimage to this day.
Her witness continues to teach us that the deepest music of a Christian life is not first heard by human ears at all.
It is the silent, hidden offering of a heart wholly given to God—a song that, once begun, this world can never entirely silence.
